title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\mathfrak g$ be a Lie algebra with a fixed basis $\{ b_1,\dots,b_n \}$ and let $\overline{\mathfrak g}$ be its complex conjugate with basis $\{ b'_1,\dots,b'_n \}$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item For each $v = \sum_j \lambda_j b_j \in \mathfrak g$, we define $\overline{v} := \sum_j \overline\lambda_j b_j' \in \overline{\mathfrak g}$.
			Similarly, if $w = \sum_j \lambda_j b_j' \in \overline{\mathfrak g}$, then we define $\overline{w} := \sum_j \overline\lambda_j b_j \in \mathfrak g$.
			In particular, $\overline b_j = b'_j$ and $\overline{b'_j} = b_j$ for all $j$.
			
			Notice that the map $\mathfrak g \to \overline{\mathfrak g} \colon v \mapsto \overline{v}$ is $\mathbb C$-semilinear, i.e., $\overline{\lambda v} = \overline{\lambda} \overline{v}$ for all $\lambda \in \mathbb C$ and all $v \in \mathfrak g$; moreover,
			\[ [\overline v, \overline w] = \overline{[v,w]} \quad \text{for all } v,w \in \mathfrak g . \]
			Similar properties hold, of course, for the map $\overline{\mathfrak g} \to \mathfrak g \colon w \mapsto \overline{w}$.
		\item If $\psi \colon \mathfrak g \to \overline{\mathfrak g}$ is a $\mathbb C$-linear Lie algebra isomorphism, then we define $\overline\psi \colon \overline{\mathfrak g} \to \mathfrak g$ as the isomorphism given by conjugating the coordinates of $\psi$ with respect to our choice of bases. Equivalently, $\overline\psi \colon \overline{\mathfrak g} \to \mathfrak g$ is defined by
			\[ \overline\psi(\overline v) := \overline{\psi(v)} \quad \text{for all } v \in \mathfrak g . \]
			Clearly, $\overline\psi$ is again a $\mathbb C$-linear Lie algebra isomorphism.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: le:realform
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{le:realform}
	The complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ has a real form if and only if there is a $\mathbb C$-linear isomorphism of Lie algebras $\psi \colon \mathfrak g \to \overline{\mathfrak g}$ with $\overline{\psi} \circ \psi = \mathrm{id}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\mathfrak g$ has a real form, then we can find a new basis $\{ f_1, \dots, f_n \}$ for $\mathfrak g$ with respect to which all structure constants $s_{ij}^k$ belong to $\mathbb R$.
	Then $\{ \overline f_1, \dots, \overline f_n \}$ is a basis for $\overline{\mathfrak g}$, and we have
	\[ [\overline f_i, \overline f_j] = \overline{[f_i, f_j]} = \overline{\sum_k s_{ij}^k f_k} = \sum_k s_{ij}^k \overline f_k \]
	since $s_{ij}^k \in \mathbb R$. Hence the $\mathbb C$-linear map $\psi \colon \mathfrak g \to \overline{\mathfrak g}$ defined by $\psi(f_i) := \overline f_i$ for all $i$ is a Lie algebra isomorphism. By definition, we have $\overline{\psi}(\overline f_i) = \overline{\psi(f_i)} = \overline{\overline{f_i}} = f_i$, so indeed $\overline{\psi} \circ \psi = \mathrm{id}$.
	
	\medskip
	
	Conversely, assume that there is a $\mathbb C$-linear isomorphism of Lie algebras $\psi \colon \mathfrak g \to \overline{\mathfrak g}$ with $\overline{\psi} \circ \psi = \mathrm{id}$.
	Composing $\psi$ with the map $\overline{\mathfrak g} \to \mathfrak g \colon w \mapsto \overline{w}$, we obtain a $\mathbb C$-semilinear automorphism $\rho \colon \mathfrak g \to \mathfrak g$, and the condition $\overline\psi \circ \psi = \mathrm{id}$ ensures that $\rho$ is an involution.
	The $\mathbb R$-subspace of fixed points of $\mathfrak g$ under $\rho$ is then a real form of $\mathfrak g$.
	(We omit the details because we do not need this reverse implication.)
head: environment

label: def
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def}
Let $\mathfrak g$ be the $9$-dimensional complex vector space with basis
\[ x_1,\ y_1,\quad x_2,\quad x_3,\ y_3,\quad x_4,\ y_4,\quad x_5,\ y_5 \]
and the antisymmetric bracket whose nonzero values on basis vectors are
\begin{alignat*}{4}
	&[x_1, y_1] = x_2, \\
	&[x_1, x_2] = x_3, && [y_1,x_2]=y_3, \\
	&[x_1, x_3] = x_4, && [y_1,y_3]=y_4, \\
	&[x_2, x_3] = x_5, && [x_2,y_3]=y_5, \\
	&[x_1, x_4] = x_5 + i y_5, \quad && [y_1, x_4] = -x_5, \quad && [x_1, y_4] = y_5, \quad && [y_1, y_4] = i x_5 + y_5.
\end{alignat*}
All other brackets of basis vectors are zero; in particular $[y_1,x_3]=[x_1,y_3]=0$.
head: environment

label: pr:lie
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To prove that $\mathfrak g$ is a Lie algebra, it suffices to check the Jacobi identity
	\[ J(a,b,c)=[a,[b,c]]+[b,[c,a]]+[c,[a,b]]=0 \]
	for basis vectors $a,b,c$.
	Because the bracket is graded and $\mathfrak g_k=0$ for $k\ge6$, $J(a,b,c)=0$ whenever the degrees add up to at least $6$.
	We may also assume that $a,b,c$ are pairwise distinct, because $J$ is alternating.
	Since $\dim\mathfrak g_1=2$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_2=1$, the only remaining triples are $(x_1,y_1,x_2)$, $(x_1,y_1,x_3)$ and $(x_1,y_1,y_3)$, and we check that
	\begin{align*}
		J(x_1,y_1,x_2) &= [x_1,y_3] - [y_1,x_3] + [x_2,x_2] = 0, \\
		J(x_1,y_1,x_3) &= [x_1,0] - [y_1,x_4] + [x_3,x_2] = 0 + x_5 - x_5 = 0, \\
		J(x_1,y_1,y_3) &= [x_1,y_4] + [y_1,0] + [y_3,x_2]=y_5+0-y_5=0.
	\end{align*}
	This proves (i).
	
	It is immediately clear from \cref{def} that $\mathfrak g$ is generated by $x_1$ and $y_1$.
	By construction, $\mathfrak g_j = [\mathfrak g_1, \mathfrak g_{j-1}]$ for all $j \geq 2$, so since $\mathfrak g$ is generated by $\mathfrak g_1$, we see by induction on~$k$ that the lower central series of $\mathfrak g$ is $\mathfrak g^k := \bigoplus_{j=k}^5 \mathfrak g_j$.
	In particular, $\mathfrak g$ is $5$-step nilpotent. This proves (ii) and (iii).
head: environment

label: pr:tau
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pr:tau}
	Let $\tau$ be the $\mathbb C$-linear map from $\mathfrak g$ to $\overline{\mathfrak g}$ given on the basis by
	\[ \tau(x_2) = x'_2, \qquad \tau(x_k) = y'_k \quad \text{and} \quad \tau(y_k) = (-1)^k x'_k \qquad (k=1,3,4,5) .\]
	Then $\tau$ is an isomorphism of Lie algebras. In particular, $\mathfrak g \cong \overline{\mathfrak g}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To show that $\tau$ is an isomorphism of Lie algebras, it suffices to check that $\tau([a,b]) = [\tau(a), \tau(b)]$ for all basis vectors $a,b$ of $\mathfrak g$, where the Lie bracket on the left hand side is in~$\mathfrak g$ and the Lie bracket on the right hand side is in $\overline{\mathfrak g}$.
	It suffices to first go over each of the $11$ non-zero brackets appearing in \cref{def} and then to check that $[\tau(a), \tau(b)] = 0$ whenever $[a,b] = 0$; the verification is straightforward.

title: Proof
body_md:
We have $[y_1,[x_1,[x_1,y_1]]]=[y_1,x_3]=0$. Applying $\varphi$ gives
	\[ [\varphi(y_1), [\varphi(x_1), [\varphi(x_1),\varphi(y_1)]]] = 0, \]
	so by the grading, we also have $[Y,[X,[X,Y]]]=0$. On the other hand, using
	$[y_1,x_3]=[x_1,y_3]=0$, $[x_1,x_3]=x_4$ and $[y_1,y_3]=y_4$, we compute
	\[
		[X,Y] = \Delta x_2,\qquad
		[X,[X,Y]] = \Delta(\alpha x_3 + \beta y_3),\qquad
		[Y,[X,[X,Y]]] = \Delta(\alpha\gamma\,x_4 + \beta\delta\,y_4).
	\]
	Hence $\alpha\gamma = \beta\delta = 0$.
	As $\Delta = \alpha\delta - \beta\gamma \neq 0$, the result follows.

label: eq:deg5
title: Proof
body_md:
We have
	\begin{multline*}
		[x_1,[x_1,[x_1,[x_1,y_1]]]] = [x_1,x_4] = x_5 + i y_5, \quad \text{with} \\
		x_5=[[x_1,y_1],[x_1,[x_1,y_1]]] \quad \text{and} \quad
			y_5=[[x_1,y_1],[y_1,[x_1,y_1]]].
	\end{multline*}
	Applying $\varphi$ and using the grading, we get
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:deg5}
		[X,[X,[X,[X,Y]]]] = [[X,Y],[X,[X,Y]]] + i\,[[X,Y],[Y,[X,Y]]].
	\end{equation}
	We now distinguish between the two different cases from \cref{le:aut level4}.
	
	Assume first that $\beta=\gamma=0$, so we have $X=\alpha x_1$ and $Y=\delta y_1$. Then each term of~\eqref{eq:deg5} is a scalar multiple of the
	corresponding bracket of $x_1$ and $y_1$, so \eqref{eq:deg5} becomes
	\[ \alpha^4\delta (x_5 + i y_5) = \alpha^3 \delta^2 x_5 + i \alpha^2\delta^3 y_5 . \]
	Comparing coefficients of $x_5$ gives $\alpha^4\delta=\alpha^3\delta^2$, i.e., $\alpha=\delta$ (because $\alpha \neq 0$ and $\delta \neq 0$).
	
	Assume next that $\alpha=\delta=0$, so we have $X=\beta y_1$ and $Y=\gamma x_1$. Then
	\begin{gather*}
		[X,Y] = -\beta\gamma x_2, \qquad
		[X,[X,Y]] = -\beta^2\gamma y_3,\qquad
		[Y,[X,Y]] = -\beta\gamma^2 x_3, \\
		[X,[X,[X,[X,Y]]]] = -\beta^4\gamma [y_1,y_4] = -\beta^4\gamma (i x_5 + y_5),
	\end{gather*}
	while the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:deg5} equals
	\[ \beta^3\gamma^2 [x_2,y_3] + i\beta^2\gamma^3[x_2,x_3] = \beta^3\gamma^2 y_5 + i \beta^2\gamma^3 x_5 . \]
	Comparing coefficients of $y_5$ and of $x_5$ gives
	\[ -\beta^4\gamma = \beta^3 \gamma^2 \quad \text{and} \quad -\beta^4\gamma = \beta^2 \gamma^3, \]
	i.e., $\beta=-\gamma$ and $\beta^2=-\gamma^2$ (because $\beta \neq 0$ and $\gamma \neq 0$), a contradiction.

label: pr:key
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pr:key}
Every automorphism $\varphi$ of $\mathfrak g$ induces a scalar multiple of the identity on $\mathfrak g/[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: This is simply a restatement of \cref{le:aut level5}.
head: environment

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
	The $9$-dimensional nilpotent complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ from Definition~\ref{def} is isomorphic to its conjugate $\overline{\mathfrak g}$, but $\mathfrak g$ has no real form.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\tau \colon \mathfrak g \to \overline{\mathfrak g}$ be the isomorphism from \cref{pr:tau}.
	Suppose that $\mathfrak g$ has a real form, and let $\psi \colon \mathfrak g \to \overline{\mathfrak g}$ be as in \cref{le:realform}.
	Then $\varphi := \tau^{-1} \circ \psi$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak g$.
	By \cref{pr:key}, $\varphi$ acts as scalar multiplication by $\lambda$ on $\mathfrak g / [\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g]$ for some $\lambda \in \mathbb C^\times$.
	Then
	\[ \varphi(x_1) = \lambda x_1 + v \quad \text{and} \quad \varphi(y_1) = \lambda y_1 + w \]
	for some $v,w \in [\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g]$, hence
	\[ \psi(x_1) = \tau(\varphi(x_1)) = \lambda \tau(x_1) + \tau(v) = \lambda y'_1 + \tau(v) \quad \text{with } \tau(v) \in [\overline{\mathfrak g}, \overline{\mathfrak g}] . \]
	Also, by the definition of $\psi$, we have
	\[ \overline\psi(y_1') = \overline{\psi(y_1)} = \overline{\tau(\varphi(y_1))} = \overline{\lambda \tau(y_1) + \tau(w)}
		= \overline{- \lambda x'_1 + \tau(w)} = - \overline\lambda x_1 + \overline{\tau(w)} , \]
	with $\overline{\tau(w)} \in [\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g]$. However, by \cref{le:realform}, we have $\overline\psi \circ \psi = \mathrm{id}$, hence
	\[ x_1 = (\overline\psi \circ \psi)(x_1) = -\lambda \overline{\lambda} x_1 + z \quad \text{with } z \in [\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g] , \]
	a contradiction because $- \lambda \overline{\lambda} = - \lvert \lambda \rvert^2 \neq 1$ and $\mathfrak g = \langle x_1, y_1 \rangle \oplus [\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g]$.
